summary: Defines a MIME content type that a mail transfer agent or gateway uses to report the result of attempts to deliver a message to one or more recipients. It is meant as a machine-processable replacement for the many ad hoc bounce formats then in use.

eli5.summary: When an email cannot be delivered, a bounce note comes back. This defines one standard format for those notes so computers can read them reliably.

questions: what is a delivery status notification
what does action failed mean in a dsn
what do smtp status codes 4.0.0 and 5.0.0 mean
subtitle: The standard, machine-readable format for the 'your message could not be delivered' notes mail servers send back.

tldr.problem: Mail systems reported delivery problems in many ad hoc bounce formats that people could read but programs could not reliably parse.
tldr.mechanism: A Delivery Status Notification (DSN) is a multipart/report MIME message whose second part, message/delivery-status, holds RFC 822-style fields: per-message fields once, then a group of per-recipient fields for each recipient.
tldr.outcome: A sender or mailing list can match each report to a message and recipient, see whether delivery failed, was delayed or succeeded, and read a transport-independent status code. The RFC obsoletes RFC 1894 and was later updated.

today: RFC 3464 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1894. It has since been updated by RFC 4865, RFC 5337 and RFC 6533, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Purpose of Delivery Status Notifications
sections.content:
This RFC defines a MIME content type, message/delivery-status, for Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs). A DSN can tell a sender about failed delivery, delayed delivery, successful delivery, or the gatewaying of a message into an environment that may not support DSNs. It is meant to be used inside the multipart/report type from RFC 3462, and it is a machine-processable replacement for the many notification styles then in use.

The purposes include informing people of delivery status independent of language, letting mail user agents associate a DSN with an earlier message, letting mailing list exploders prune subscribers whose delivery repeatedly fails, carrying notifications through gateways to foreign systems such as X.400, and giving remote MTA maintainers enough detail to understand an error.

Only the format is defined here. The SMTP extension to request such notifications is in a separate memo, RFC 3461.
sections.eli5: A bounce note should say what happened, to whom, and why, in a form both people and computers can understand.

sections.title: The Shape of a DSN Message
sections.content:
A DSN is a MIME message with a top-level type of multipart/report and a report-type parameter of delivery-status. It has up to three parts: a human-readable explanation, the message/delivery-status part, and optionally the original message or part of it.

The DSN MUST be addressed, in both the header and the envelope, to the return address from the original message's envelope. Over SMTP the envelope sender of a DSN MUST be the null address, MAIL FROM:<>, so that DSNs cannot cause mail loops. The From header SHOULD name a human responsible for the Reporting MTA site, such as Postmaster.

The body of message/delivery-status uses RFC 822 header-field syntax. Per-message fields come first, followed by a blank line, then one or more groups of per-recipient fields, each group preceded by a blank line. Field names are case-insensitive, and 7bit encoding MUST be used. One DSN describes exactly one message, but may cover several recipients.
sections.eli5: A bounce message has a part for humans, a part with a neat form for computers, and sometimes a copy of the original letter.

sections.title: Per-Message Fields
sections.content:
Per-message fields apply to the whole report and may appear at most once. Only Reporting-MTA is required.

  • Reporting-MTA: the MTA that attempted the delivery, relay or gateway operation described. It is not necessarily the MTA that sent the DSN, for example when a gateway translates a foreign report.
  • Original-Envelope-Id: an identifier for the submission transaction. It is case-sensitive and is not the Message-Id.
  • DSN-Gateway: names the gateway that translated a foreign notification. It MUST appear in such a DSN and MUST NOT appear otherwise.
  • Received-From-MTA: the MTA the message came from.
  • Arrival-Date: when the message reached the Reporting MTA, with a numeric time zone.

Fields that name MTAs or addresses use a type;value form, such as dns; cs.utk.edu, so the DSN does not assume any particular address or naming scheme.
sections.eli5: The top of the form says who is reporting and which delivery job this is, like the case number on a help-desk ticket.

sections.title: Per-Recipient Fields
sections.content:
Each recipient gets its own group of fields. Final-Recipient, Action and Status are required. Original-Recipient carries the address exactly as the sender gave it and should be included only when the transport provides it. Remote-MTA, Diagnostic-Code, Last-Attempt-Date, Final-Log-ID and Will-Retry-Until are optional.

The Action field has five values: failed (abandoned, no more notices expected), delayed (still trying), delivered (reached the specified address, which does not mean it was read), relayed (passed to an environment that will not report back) and expanded (delivered and then forwarded to several addresses, not a terminal state).

The Status field is a transport-independent code of the form digit.digits.digits. Its first number says whether the attempt succeeded (2), is a persistent temporary failure (4) or a permanent failure (5). The second number indicates the probable source of the problem and the third a precise condition, if known. The initial set of codes is defined in RFC 3463. Diagnostic-Code keeps the transport's own code, for example an SMTP reply, since the Status code may be less precise.
sections.eli5: Each person you wrote to gets a line saying what happened to their letter: delivered, still trying, or gave up. A short code tells the type of problem.

sections.title: Type Registries and Extension Fields
sections.content:
Fields that carry addresses, status codes and MTA names have a type sub-field: address-type (for example rfc822), diagnostic-type (for example smtp) and MTA-name-type (for example dns). IANA keeps a registry of these types. Type names starting with X- are reserved for experimental use and are never registered.

New per-message or per-recipient fields may be defined later. Names beginning with X- will never become standard fields, while other names MUST be registered with IANA and published in an RFC. Extension fields can carry details from foreign systems, transport-specific diagnostics or MTA-specific data, such as a log entry reference to help the MTA maintainer.

An appendix gives non-binding guidance for gateways that convert between DSNs and other mail systems' reports, falling back to generic codes such as 2.0.0, 4.0.0 and 5.0.0 when needed.
sections.eli5: The form has room for new boxes, and each kind of address or code says which language it is written in so the reader knows how to understand it.

sections.title: Conformance and Mailing Lists
sections.content:
A minimal implementation need only generate the Reporting-MTA field, plus Final-Recipient, Action and Status for each recipient. Generating the other fields when appropriate is strongly recommended. MTAs and gateways MUST NOT generate Original-Recipient unless the transport provides the sender's original address.

Each sender-specified recipient address SHOULD result in at most one delivered or failed DSN. Delivery to a mailing list exploder counts as final delivery.

An appendix explains how a list can use DSNs: send list mail with an envelope return address that receives non-delivery reports, then read the Original-Recipient, Status and Action fields. It advises not to remove a subscriber because of delayed reports or a single failure, but only after failure persists over a period of time.
sections.eli5: A mailing list can read these notes and drop addresses that keep failing, but it should wait and make sure it is not a one-day hiccup.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DSNs can be forged as easily as ordinary mail. The RFC lists falsified delivery or non-delivery notices, forged recipient or Remote-MTA information, and unsolicited DSNs, and says programs that use DSNs automatically should take precautions against denial-of-service attacks.

Confidentiality matters too: a recipient who auto-forwards mail may not want the forwarding address revealed. MTA authors are encouraged to let users keep it private, for example by omitting Remote-* or extension fields, using the null return path, or issuing a delivered or relayed DSN instead. Finally, a failed DSN is not a guarantee that the message was not received, because an SMTP race condition can duplicate a message and one copy may succeed while another fails.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a fake bounce note, and a note saying 'failed' might be wrong. So computers should be careful about trusting these notes too much.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC's appendix includes examples translated from real bounces, marked as illustration only. The simplest shows a message that could not be delivered after repeated attempts. The DSN part names the reporting MTA and gives one recipient with action failed and status 4.0.0, along with the SMTP diagnostic and the time of the last attempt.

Other examples show a DSN with several recipients where some failed and one was delayed, a DSN gatewayed from a foreign system, and a delay report that returns no copy of the original message.
sections.eli5: It is like a filled-in sample form, so you can see what a real note looks like.

viz.caption: FIELDS FROM THE RFC'S SIMPLE DSN EXAMPLE

data.title: message/delivery-status part
data.code:
Reporting-MTA: dns; cs.utk.edu

Original-Recipient: rfc822;louisl@larry.slip.umd.edu
Final-Recipient: rfc822;louisl@larry.slip.umd.edu
Action: failed
Status: 4.0.0
Diagnostic-Code: smtp; 426 connection timed out
Last-Attempt-Date: Thu, 7 Jul 1994 17:15:49 -0400

viz.caption: THE FIVE VALUES OF THE ACTION FIELD

items.label: Not delivered
items.desc: The Reporting MTA abandoned delivery; no further notices are expected.

items.label: Still trying
items.desc: Not yet delivered, but attempts continue; more notices may follow.

items.label: Delivered
items.desc: Reached the specified address; does not mean it was read. Terminal.

items.label: Handed on
items.desc: Passed to an environment that does not report delivery.

items.label: Forwarded to several
items.desc: Delivered, then forwarded to multiple addresses; not terminal.
